findings.source_passage: Seventh month: Pleasing appearance and nice manners so striking that am promoted to waiting on the Sisters!
findings.source_locator: Tuppence's abridged biography, seventh month entry
findings.why_it_matters: The self-mocking comic voice of the biography section is one of the chapter's most distinctive passages; the draft collapses months 5-7 into 'promotions ensued: drying, potatoes, bread and butter, wardmaid with mop and pail, then waiting at table, then on the Sisters!' losing the specific comic phrasing that makes the seventh month funny.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the seventh month entry verbatim: 'Seventh month: Pleasing appearance and nice manners so striking that am promoted to waiting on the Sisters!'

findings.source_passage: How are the mighty fallen! Ninth month: Promoted to sweeping out wards, where I found a friend of my childhood
findings.source_locator: Tuppence's abridged biography, eighth-ninth month entries
findings.why_it_matters: The exclamatory 'How are the mighty fallen!' is a distinctively voice-rich comic flourish within the mock-heroic biography; the draft drops it entirely, weakening the ironic register of the passage.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'How are the mighty fallen!' between 'Mop and pail again!' and 'Ninth:' to preserve the mock-heroic rhetorical escalation.

findings.source_passage: The meeting was affecting! Tenth month: Reproved by matron for visiting the pictures
findings.source_locator: Tuppence's abridged biography, ninth-tenth month transition
findings.why_it_matters: 'The meeting was affecting!' is a characteristically dry Christie comic aside; its omission removes a beat of ironic understatement central to Tuppence's voice.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'The meeting was affecting!' after the introduction of Lieutenant Thomas Beresford in the ninth month entry.

findings.source_passage: she has that delightful early Victorian view that short skirts and smoking are immoral. You can imagine what a thorn in the flesh I am to him! He just heaved a sigh of relief when the war took me off.
findings.source_locator: Tuppence's speech about going home, after 'Father's a dear'
findings.why_it_matters: This passage establishes Tuppence's sardonic self-awareness and her generational-cultural position with precision; the draft reduces it to a flat clause ('short skirts and smoking are immoral'), losing the 'thorn in the flesh' image and the sigh-of-relief line that characterise the relationship.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the fuller speech: 'He has that delightful early Victorian view that short skirts and smoking are immoral. You can imagine what a thorn in the flesh I am to him! He just heaved a sigh of relief when the war took me off.'

findings.source_passage: I always help old ladies over crossings, and pick up parcels for old gentlemen, in case they should turn out to be eccentric millionaires. But not one of them has ever asked me my name--and quite a lot never said 'Thank you.'
findings.source_locator: Tuppence's speech on 'being left' money, before the marriage section
findings.why_it_matters: The comic image of Tuppence tirelessly assisting elderly strangers in hopes of inheritance is a charming character detail and period-specific joke; the draft strips it to 'the old ladies I help over crossings never even ask my name,' losing the parcels, the eccentric millionaires, and the wry 'quite a lot never said Thank you.'
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the fuller version: 'I always help old ladies over crossings, and pick up parcels for old gentlemen, in case they should turn out to be eccentric millionaires. But not one of them has ever asked me my name--and quite a lot never said Thank you.'

findings.source_passage: Now, if I see a man in a fur coat come out of the Ritz I can't rush up to him and say: 'Look here, you're rich. I'd like to know you.'
findings.source_locator: Tuppence's speech on why she can't marry a rich man, after 'you could marry a rich girl'
findings.why_it_matters: This is a characteristic Tuppence comic line—direct, self-aware, period-voiced—that the draft removes entirely, replacing it with no equivalent, slightly weakening the repartee.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the fur-coat-Ritz line before the discussion of how Tommy might meet a rich girl.

findings.source_passage: it struck me as such a romantic phrase to come across in the middle of musty old figures. It's got an Elizabethan flavour about it--makes one think of galleons and doubloons.
findings.source_locator: Tuppence explaining 'joint venture', before Tommy names the company
findings.why_it_matters: The draft keeps 'Elizabethan flavour--galleons and doubloons' but drops the preceding context ('such a romantic phrase to come across in the middle of musty old figures'), which grounds the joke in Tuppence's bookkeeping past and makes the romanticism funnier by contrast.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore: 'It struck me as such a romantic phrase to come across in the middle of musty old figures' before 'It's got an Elizabethan flavour.'

summary: No high-severity losses; four medium-severity findings (voice flattening in the comic biography section and Tuppence's home-life speech) and three low-severity losses, falling just below the regeneration threshold, but the draft should be revised to restore the suppressed comic voice in the biography passage and the 'thorn in the flesh' / 'sigh of relief' lines.
